primary_sources: Rudyard Kipling, "The White Man's Burden," McClure's Magazine, February 1899

stimulus.source_note: Rudyard Kipling, "The White Man's Burden," McClure's Magazine, February 1899, public domain.
stimulus.text: "Take up the White Man's burden — Send forth the best ye breed — Go bind your sons to exile To serve your captives' need; To wait in heavy harness, On fluttered folk and wild — Your new-caught, sullen peoples, Half-devil and half-child. Take up the White Man's burden — In patience to abide, To veil the threat of terror And check the show of pride; By open speech and simple, An hundred times made plain To seek another's profit, And work another's gain." — Rudyard Kipling, "The White Man's Burden," McClure's Magazine, February 1899

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim excerpt (first two stanzas) from Rudyard Kipling, "The White Man's Burden," McClure's Magazine, February 1899, public domain.
stem: Kipling's call to "serve your captives' need" appealed most directly to which group of Americans?

options.text: Missionaries who saw empire as a field for conversion
Southern Democrats who feared an influx of Filipinos
options.misconception: Those critics opposed empire because they feared Filipinos entering American life. Kipling's call to serve them is the opposite impulse.

options.text: Labor leaders who feared competition from colonial workers
options.misconception: Labor critics opposed empire because colonial workers might undercut American wages. They did not hear a call to serve.

options.text: Isolationists who wanted no foreign commitments
options.misconception: Isolationists rejected overseas rule entirely. A call to serve captives abroad is not their language.

rationales.A: Background: missionary leaders backed empire because it opened new peoples to convert. Kipling's language of service and uplift is their argument in poetic form.
rationales.B: Those critics opposed empire because they feared Filipinos entering American life. Kipling's call to serve them is the opposite impulse.
rationales.C: Labor critics opposed empire because colonial workers might undercut American wages. They did not hear a call to serve.
rationales.D: Isolationists rejected overseas rule entirely. A call to serve captives abroad is not their language.
rationales.general:
1. Read the verb. "Serve" frames ruling as helping, not conquering.
2. Ask who already talked that way. Background: missionary leaders backed empire because it opened new peoples to convert.
3. Test the other groups. Each opposed empire for its own reasons, and none used the language of service.
4. Put it together. Kipling's uplift language and the missionary case for empire are the same argument in different words.
Remember: the same policy can wear many arguments, so match the words to the group that used them.
